record.file_problem: Whole post and comments are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The post analyzes downstream benchmark accuracy against held-out next-token loss and extrapolates performance using a different measure and analysis from the original pretraining-loss scaling studies. It also calculates how fit choices affect its compute estimates.
record.gate_note: The post uses Kaplan et al.'s loss scaling laws but does not independently measure language-model pretraining loss across sizes, tokens, or compute, or test compute-optimal allocations. Cited loss-scaling results and speculative cost and automation projections are not independent result rows. The reported downstream benchmark trends and the post's own fit-sensitivity calculation are included.
record.test_reason: The post fits normalized few-shot accuracy for 8 GPT-3 sizes against validation next-token loss. It checks whether the largest model stays on the trend from the smaller ones. That bears directly on V6, using a different method from the originals. Its loss scaling laws are taken from Kaplan et al. and are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes that GPT-3 175B's benchmark performance is in line with trends from smaller models, neither breaking nor accelerating them. Arithmetic and Scramble jump sharply, which the author ascribes to narrow tasks with a trick, and ANLI barely improves. Projected near-optimal benchmark performance is at least about 3 orders of magnitude more compute away, more likely 5-6 OOM if scaling naively. All long-range extrapolations are called tentative and dependent on scaling-law choice.
record.recipe_differences: Applies prior next-token-loss scaling laws to extrapolate downstream few-shot benchmark performance rather than measuring pretraining loss scaling itself; uses benchmark accuracy-versus-loss trends and selected fit values.
record.method_sensitivity: The category aggregation, choice of linear versus sigmoid performance curves, and choice between Kaplan et al. fit values affect the interpretation or extrapolated estimates.

fits_no_version.finding: Using Kaplan et al.'s Figure 1 fit values instead of the page 11 values makes the post's projected FLOP to reach a given loss about 2-5x larger.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute forecasts derived from published loss scaling laws are sensitive, by small multiples, to which reported fit of the same study is used.

record.problems: The analysis relies on measurements from 8 model sizes and reported plots rather than numerical results reproduced in the post text. The author calls long-range extrapolations shaky and notes that alternative fit values produce estimates about 2-5x larger. The downstream-to-pretraining-loss relationship is an assumption of the procedure.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results left out. The post's cited loss-scaling results and its speculative cost and automation projections were not included as independent findings.

untested.parts: Loss power laws are taken from Kaplan et al.; no loss is measured across N, D or C.
No loss extrapolation is checked. The long-range benchmark projections are forecasts, not tests.
Compute-optimal allocation is assumed via L(N,D) with one epoch, not tested.

Only GPT-3's 8 sizes are covered, all trained on the same 300B tokens, in a few-shot setting. The claim that loss predicts performance across different N/D trade-offs is assumed, not tested. Predictability beyond 175B is projected, not observed.
No refit and no new comparison of fitting choices. The L(C) versus L(N,D) inconsistency is cited from Kaplan et al. and Henighan et al.

missing.what: Aggregation choice: averaging over all benchmarks (OpenAI-style) shows a sharper acceleration at the largest model than averaging over categories. This is because arithmetic contributes 10 benchmarks versus a mean of about 4.5 per category. Smoothness of the aggregate downstream curve therefore depends on weighting.

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog post with no numeric values in the text; all rows are qualitative readings of plots. The 8 models share 300B training tokens, so the loss-to-performance mapping is tested only along model size. Linear and sigmoid projections beyond 175B are forecasts and are not treated as rows. The V7 label from the record is dropped because R5 only propagates the original source's own fits.

versions.untested_parts: The post uses prior scaling laws to extrapolate loss; it does not test whether held-out pretraining loss follows power laws across parameters, tokens, or compute.
The post examines downstream benchmark performance against loss, not whether power laws fitted on small runs predict the held-out loss of much larger runs.
The post assumes or applies prior scaling laws for estimating compute and does not test how loss-minimizing parameter and token counts scale with compute.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
The analysis concerns the reported GPT-3 few-shot benchmarks and validation loss; it does not establish predictability for other downstream tasks, models, or evaluation regimes.

The post calculates sensitivity of its compute estimates to selected scaling-law fit values, but does not refit exponents on new experiments or independently test compute-optimal splits. Discussion of disagreements between laws relies on prior work.

relationships.reason: Accuracy rises roughly linearly in log-loss at similar rates across categories, and GPT-3 175B lies on the trend set by smaller models (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increases roughly linearly as log-loss decreases at similar rates across most categories, with GPT-3 175B following the smaller-model trend.

relationships.reason: These are flat, then jump sharply (R2, R3), or barely leave chance at the largest size (R4). They could not be predicted from the smaller models' trend, and the author does not extrapolate them linearly.
relationships.display_finding: Arithmetic and Scramble stayed flat before sharp jumps, while ANLI barely exceeded chance at the largest size, preventing linear extrapolation from smaller models.
